slides.text: SQL basics: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY
slides.say: Data Science from Scratch, lesson seventeen: SQL basics. Select, where, and group by.

slides.text: Much of the world's data lives in databases
slides.sub: SQL is how you ask them questions
slides.say: A lot of business data, like customers and transactions, lives in relational databases. SQL is the standard language for asking those databases questions, so it's one of the most useful skills a data scientist can have.
Every query starts with select. You list the columns you want, then say which table they come from, using from.
Where filters the rows. Here we keep only transactions where the amount is greater than one thousand. Rows that don't match are left out.

slides.text:
SELECT city, COUNT(*), AVG(amount)
FROM transactions
GROUP BY city
slides.say: Group by puts rows into groups and gives you one summary row per group. Combine it with functions like count, sum, or average, and you get, say, the number of transactions and the average amount for each city.

slides.text:
WHERE filters rows before grouping.
HAVING filters groups after.
slides.say: One thing that trips beginners up: where filters individual rows before they are grouped. To filter the groups themselves, like cities with more than fifty transactions, you use having.

slides.text: Choose columns, filter rows, then summarise groups.
slides.say: So the takeaway: select chooses columns, where filters rows, and group by summarises groups.

slides.text: Train/test split: why we hide data from the model

summary: SELECT chooses columns and FROM names the table, WHERE filters individual rows, and GROUP BY with functions like COUNT, SUM and AVG produces one summary row per group. Use HAVING to filter groups after grouping.
practice: Draw a small table of 8 transactions with columns city and amount. By hand, work out the result of: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM transactions WHERE amount > 500 GROUP BY city.
